scenes.heading: Lambda Architecture
scenes.subheading: Batch plus speed, merged at serving
scenes.narration: The Lambda architecture combines a batch layer for accurate historical results with a speed layer for low-latency recent data, merging both at a serving layer.

scenes.heading: The three layers
bullets: Batch layer recomputes accurate views from raw data
Speed layer processes recent events with low latency
Serving layer merges batch and real-time views
Raw immutable log is the source of truth
scenes.narration: The batch layer periodically recomputes comprehensive, accurate views over the entire immutable dataset. The speed layer processes only the most recent events in near real time to fill the gap since the last batch run. The serving layer merges the batch views with the real-time views so queries see a complete picture. Underneath it all sits an append-only master dataset that acts as the immutable source of truth.

scenes.heading: Data flowing through Lambda
scenes.narration: New events are appended to an immutable master log. The batch layer periodically reprocesses that whole log to produce authoritative batch views. In parallel, the speed layer incrementally processes just the events that arrived since the last batch run, producing approximate real-time views. The serving layer combines the batch and real-time views, and when the next batch run completes it supersedes the speed layer output, so any errors self-correct over time.

scenes.heading: Batch layer vs speed layer
scenes.narration: The batch layer is accurate and complete because it reprocesses everything, but its results are hours behind and it is conceptually simple. The speed layer delivers results within seconds by handling only recent data, but that incremental processing is approximate and its code is more complex. The tension between them is exactly why Lambda maintains two code paths, which is its main drawback: the same logic must be implemented and kept in sync in both layers.

scenes.heading: Why Lambda self-corrects
bullets: Next batch run overwrites recent views
Errors in the speed layer wash out
scenes.narration: A key strength of Lambda is that it self-heals. The speed layer's approximate results are only temporary, filling the gap since the last batch run. When the next batch run completes, its authoritative output overwrites those recent views. This means any bug or approximation error in the speed layer is automatically washed out on the next cycle. All of this rests on the immutable master log, which lets the batch layer recompute correct results from scratch whenever needed.

scenes.heading: The cost of two code paths
bullets: Same logic written twice, in two systems
Behavior can drift between the paths
This is why many teams prefer Kappa
scenes.narration: The main drawback of Lambda is operational. The same business logic must be implemented twice, once in a batch framework and once in a streaming framework, often in different languages and systems. Over time the two implementations can drift and produce subtly different results, which is hard to debug. You also pay double for testing and maintenance. This duplication is precisely the pain that the Kappa architecture set out to remove by using a single streaming path for everything.

scenes.text: Lambda buys correctness plus freshness at the cost of duplicated logic; reach for it only when both truly matter.
scenes.narration: Lambda delivers both eventual correctness and real-time freshness, but it does so by maintaining duplicate logic in two layers, so reach for it only when you genuinely need both guarantees and otherwise consider the simpler Kappa approach.
